messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Minh was 26 when he first came for help, a South Eastern Asian man who had been divorced for a little over a year and was working as a bank teller in a busy branch where he spent long hours behind a counter greeting customers, counting cash, and trying to keep his attention fixed on the rhythm of the day. Two years earlier, while he was commuting home after an evening shift in a downtown area, a bomb had detonated several blocks away during a crowded public event. In the confusion that followed, sirens filled the streets, people ran in every direction, and Minh was swept into the crush of terrified strangers. He remembered the abrupt force of the blast, the choking smoke, and the sight of injured people being helped onto the pavement. What stayed with him most was not only the noise and chaos but the split-second fear that he might die before he could understand what was happening, and the shame he later felt for the way he reacted when others needed help. He had not been injured, but he left that area with the conviction that he had failed himself in a way he could not fully put into words.

In the weeks after the bombing, Minh tried to push the event out of his mind. He worked extra shifts whenever they were offered and volunteered for overtime at the bank, staying busy from opening to closing so that there would be no quiet moments in which the images could return. He began taking on extra tasks that other employees avoided, staying late to balance drawers and reorganize paperwork long after his coworkers had gone home. When he was at work, he could keep himself contained; when he was alone in his apartment, the memories crowded in more easily, so he filled every hour he could. Even so, he found that certain moments pierced that effort. A sudden bang in the street, the wail of emergency sirens, or a dense crowd near the subway entrance could send his attention snapping back to that day, and he would feel a surge of tension as if he were again in the middle of the scene. At the bank, the sound of a security door slamming or a raised voice from a customer could make him look up sharply, his body already braced.

Over time, Minh began living with a narrow, guarded sense of safety. He woke during the night to check whether he was safe, sometimes sitting up in bed and listening for sounds outside his window, other times scanning his apartment before trying to sleep again. If he heard footsteps in the hallway, he would check the peephole and look behind him more than once before stepping into the corridor. Even on the walk from the train to his apartment, he repeatedly glanced over his shoulder, telling himself that he was just being careful, though he rarely felt reassured for long. He became more irritable with people around him, especially when they moved too quickly or asked questions when he was already tense. At work, his anger sometimes surfaced as clipped replies to customers or abrupt exchanges with coworkers, which left him embarrassed afterward but no less on edge the next time. He came to believe that the version of himself he once trusted was gone, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him before the bombing. Before, he had seen himself as steady, disciplined, and able to protect his family; afterward, he felt changed in a way that made even ordinary decisions seem less certain. He also carried a painful sense that he had acted in ways that went against who he was. In the chaos after the blast, he had focused on getting himself out, and although he knew fear had narrowed his thinking, he could not stop returning to the feeling that he should have done more. That thought sat heavily with him, especially because he had been raised to value responsibility and composure.

As the months went by, Minh grew less interested in closeness with other people. He kept conversations at work polite and brief, declined invitations to meet colleagues after shifts, and found himself distancing from anyone who seemed to want emotional openness. After his marriage ended, he did not try to rebuild intimacy, telling himself that it was safer not to let anyone get too close. He worried that if he were known too well, others would see how unsettled he had become and judge him for it. The divorce had already left him feeling exposed, and the bombing seemed to have deepened his sense that he could not depend on himself to remain calm, thoughtful, or reliable. He was especially troubled by how often he second-guessed even simple choices, as if his own judgment had become an uncertain thing.

By the time he sought therapy, Minh had reached a point where the effort of keeping everything contained was becoming harder to manage. He still worked long hours, still tried to stay ahead of his thoughts, and still told himself that sleeping lightly and watching his surroundings was just common sense, but he was tired of feeling tense in his own body and ashamed of the anger that surfaced without warning. What finally brought him in was the realization that he was living as if danger could appear at any moment, even in ordinary places like his apartment hallway, the street outside his building, or the bank lobby where he spent most of his days. He hoped that treatment might help him feel more like himself again, though what frightened him most was the possibility that he would always feel unsafe, uncertain, and separated from the person he used to believe he could be.
